source.title: Pattern separation in the human hippocampal CA3 and dentate gyrus.

confidence_rationale: High-resolution human fMRI placing the separation bias specifically in CA3/DG and the COMPLETION bias in CA1/subiculum -- corroborates the rodent result in humans and, importantly, localises the separation/completion division that MECH-147's circuit depends on. Lower transfer risk than rodent work; held below 0.85 by fMRI's indirect read of subfield computation.
failure_signatures: fMRI BOLD is an indirect, population-level proxy for the underlying separation computation; the study infers separation vs completion from repetition-related activity, not from single-unit decorrelation.

mapping.source_claim_statement: High-resolution fMRI during incidental encoding shows a strong bias toward pattern separation limited to CA3/dentate gyrus, while CA1, subiculum, and entorhinal/parahippocampal cortices show a bias toward pattern completion.
mapping.ree_translation: Human confirmation of MECH-147's separation stage AND its completion-set partner in one map: separation is a CA3/DG property, completion a CA1/EC property. For REE this argues the separation layer and a completion/readout stage are anatomically distinct sub-computations that must both exist -- separation alone is not the whole disambiguation circuit.
mapping.mapping_caveat: BOLD signal infers separation vs completion from how activity changes to similar-vs-repeated lures; it does not directly measure the sparse-code decorrelation. The subfield assignment is high-resolution but still a population proxy.
mapping.source_context: Human adults, 1.5mm isotropic high-resolution fMRI during an incidental memory-encoding task with similar lure stimuli.

confidence_components.notes: Human data lowers transfer risk relative to rodent ephys. Mapping fidelity strong for localising separation-vs-completion; fmri indirectness caps source_quality.
